about: The Prologue of Saint John (John 1:1–14), read at the Gospel side at the end of Mass. Before reading, the priest signs the altar or book and then his forehead, lips, and breast. He genuflects at “Et Verbum caro factum est”.

s01.narrative: Then the priest, at the Gospel side with hands joined, says:

s04.narrative: And signing with the sign of the cross first the altar or the book, then himself on the forehead, the lips and the breast, the priest says:

s05.translation: The beginning of the holy Gospel according to John.

s07.narrative: With his hands joined the priest continues:

s08.translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by Him, and without Him was made nothing that was made: in Him was Life, and the Life was the Light of men; and the Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend It.

s09.translation: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. This man came for a witness, to bear witness of the Light, that all might believe through him. He was not the Light, but was to bear witness of the Light.

s10.translation: It was the true Light, which enlightens every man that comes into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not. But as many as received Him, to them He gave power to be made the sons of God, to them that believe in His name, who are born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

s12.translation: And the Word was made flesh,

s14.translation: and dwelt among us; and we saw His glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

w007.function: Nominative in a nominal announcement without an expressed verb.

w012.function: Nominal response without an expressed verb.

w018.function: “Verbum” is neuter. In the Greek text of Jn 1:1 it corresponds to “lógos”.

w022.function: “Apud” governs the accusative and here means “with” or “in the presence of”.

w036.note: The gender is open. The only grammatical antecedent is Verbum, which is neuter, but the tradition reads a masculine here, of the Person. This edition takes the masculine.

w037.function: With “sunt” (w038) it forms the perfect passive: facta sunt — “were made”.

w041.note: The gender is open, as at w036. This edition takes the masculine.

w044.function: Nominative subject in the preceding clause.

w049.note: The gender is open, as at w036. This edition takes the masculine.

w069.function: A passive participle in the nominative, agreeing with “homo” (w068).

w072.function: Dative of possession: “to whom the name was John”, that is, whose name was John.

w077.function: Perfect, not present: the form is the same for both, but the narrative runs in the past — “Fuit” (w067), “erat” (w074).

w082.function: Imperfect subjunctive in a purpose clause after “ut” (w080).

w107.function: Accusative agreeing with “hóminem” (w106): in the Latin sentence it is the man who comes into the world.

w126.function: Neuter plural adjective used substantively: “His own things”.

w129.function: Masculine plural adjective used substantively: “His own people”. Compare neuter “própria” (w126).

w164.function: A deponent participle: passive in form, active in meaning. With “sunt” (w165) it forms the perfect — they were born.

w168.function: Feminine predicate nominative. Neuter “factum” (w169) agrees with “Verbum” (w167).

w181.function: Adjective used substantively in the genitive: “of the Only-begotten”.

w184.function: The form is neuter nominative and accusative at once. This edition reads a nominative referring back to “Verbum” (w167), with the genitives “grátiæ” (w185) and “veritátis” (w187) depending on it. The Glossa interlinearis reads an accusative, the object of “vídimus”.

function_citations.title: Glossa ordinaria on John
function_citations.locator: John 1:14, plenum gratiae et veritatis (interlinear gloss, which reads an accusative)

w184.note: The form decides nothing between nominative and accusative, and the old commentators read it both ways. This edition takes the nominative and marks the doubt.
